title: 'High risk' of lake bursting and causing second flood, warns China
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
China has warned there is a "high risk" a lake that formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach its banks, causing a second flood downstream.

The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area, which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river.

As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. Officials said that three million cubic metres of water was expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and the weekend, posing a "high risk of breach".

But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain out naturally over time.

China's Ministry of Water resources said that the barrier lake - a body of water formed when debris dams up a river - had formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers.

It is near the Langtang Lirung peak where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood.

The barrier lake had started to overflow on Thursday. Then on Friday morning, a Chinese military drone captured footage of an avalanche on a snow-capped mountain which deposited an estimated 50,000 cubic metres of ice debris into the barrier lake.

Authorities issued warnings and orders to prepare for emergency evacuations. Rescue work was suspended as most of the Chinese emergency services stopped at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port.

This was because the barrier lake at that time was "overflowing non-stop", which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows, according to a CCTV report.

But by Friday afternoon, state media reported that the "risk from the upstream barrier lake had come under control" and that rescue operations had resumed.

Authorities have since sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions, and drones have been flown in to drop off equipment and supplies.

title: Hundreds dead as nearly 1,000 remain missing in massive Nepal-Tibet flood
author: Abc News
content:
The wall of water that descended caused destruction at least 62 miles downriver.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026.

LONDON -- The death toll continues to climb days after massive flash flooding obliterated parts of the Nepal-Tibet border region on Wednesday, with at least 682 bodies recovered across the region and over 3,000 people missing, authorities said Saturday.

As search and rescue efforts continued in Nepal on Saturday, authorities said at least 7,514 people had been rescued, including 227 foreign nationals, according to the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority.

At least 219 injured people have received treatment or have been discharged as of Saturday, according to the disaster management authority.

A drone view of a bridge damaged by flash flooding along the Tadi River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026. Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo

In Nepal, 675 people have been reported dead and 2,498 others remain missing, according to the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority.

In the Chinese region of Tibet, seven people have been reported dead and 554 others have been reported missing, according to China state news agency Xinhua.

Firefighters conduct search and rescue operations along a river, after a mudslide in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, Aug. 29, 2026. CNS Photo via Reuters

Among the missing are 90 Americans as of Friday, according to a State Department spokesperson. The department confirmed Friday that five Americans had been evacuated, up from three on Thursday.

The number of people considered missing has fluctuated significantly as recovery efforts have accelerated.

"There is no higher priority for us than the safety of American citizens," the State Department said in a statement on Saturday, saying U.S. embassies in Nepal and China were working to assist Americans and support disaster relief efforts.

In the statement, the State Department said it was "standing with the people of Nepal" and would provide "$3.6 million worth of life-saving humanitarian assistance, including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households."

People rescued and airlifted from flood-affected areas arrive at Maithali Barrack, an army training centre that serves as a primary base for airlifting survivors, following flash floods and a mudslide in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

The burial of severely damaged and unidentifiable bodies and body parts began in the districts of Chitwan and Nawalparasi on Saturday and will be expanded to other affected areas, Dr. Samir Kumar Adhikari Saturday, a spokesperson for Nepal's Ministry of Health, told ABC News.

Nepal's Prime Minister Baken Shah said the government would preserve DNA samples and other identifying evidence from bodies that cannot be identified before proceeding with their burial. This is so they can be potentially matched with family members in the future, Adhikari said.

"Only bodies that cannot be identified will be managed by the government after preserving DNA and other evidence that could help establish their identity," Shah said in a post on social media.

The remains of those identified by their families are being returned to their relatives, Shah said.

Bodies that can still be identified are being preserved in freezers, Adhikari said.

Adhikari said Nepal does not have the capacity to store such a large number of severely damaged remains for an extended period. His working estimate is that around 650 bodies and body parts have been recovered; many of the remains were swept far downstream and can no longer be identified visually.

Nepal is coordinating forensic efforts with India and China, while Israeli experts are expected to arrive in the country. Additional international specialists are already providing assistance remotely, Adhikari said.

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district along the border with Tibet at around 8:40 a.m. local time Wednesday, authorities said. The flooding inundated areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

The deadly wall of water that descended from the mountains on the border between Nepal and Tibet caused destruction at least 62 miles downriver from the border in Nepal, an ABC News analysis of verified video and satellite images shows.

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 12 miles northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China frontier, according to Nepal Disaster Management.

This image taken by Planet Labs on Oct. 1, 2025, shows an overview of the China-Nepal border and Gyirong Port/Rasuwagadhi border post. | This image taken by Planet Labs PBC shows Rasuwagadi, on the border between Nepal and Tibet on Aug. 28, 2026. 2026 Planet Labs PBC via AFP via Getty Images | 2026 Planet Labs PBC via AP

A 5.2-magnitude landslide was registered in Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The seismic activity from the landslide was initially erroneously reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, the agency said. It is unclear what triggered the landslide.

A geophysicist at Columbia University in New York told ABC News it appeared a landslide in the Himalayas took away a large glacier, or parts of one, in the mountain pass.

The initial location of the glacier was a cliff about 16,000 feet high. The debris avalanche, or landslide, slid down 6,000 feet on the slope, the USGS said.

Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris in Devighat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, on Aug. 29, 2026, following the Aug. 26 flash floods. Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo

While it will take time to determine how severe the landslide was, the USGS estimated that more than 100 million cubic meters of ice, rock and debris were displaced in the event, Ben Mirus, a research geologist with the agency, said Thursday.

Siddarth Venkatachalam, 30, told ABC News he had spoken to his mother just two or three hours before she went missing in the floods, as it was her birthday. Venkatachalam's mother was on a trip with his father and aunt, who are also among the Americans missing in Nepal.

"They were like excited for this trip," Venkatachalam said, visibly in shock. "It was like a spiritual, religious like trek they'd been looking forward to and preparing for."

Damaged houses are seen along the river Trishuli following flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 29, 2026. Dar Yasin/AP Photo

The family said the three were located with Life360 on a bridge on the Tibetan border just before the flood.

In a statement, Nepal's Office of the Prime Minister expressed "deep sorrow" over the loss of life.

"Offering heartfelt tribute to all those who lost their lives in this natural disaster, it extends its sincere condolences to the bereaved families and relatives," the statement shared on social media said.

Meanwhile, the Nepali government on Thursday established an "Emergency Control Room ... to facilitate search, rescue, information verification and consular assistance in respect of foreign nationals affected by, missing in, or otherwise connected to the flood incident," according to Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

TOPSHOT - An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Nepal's disaster agency said that 823 people remained out of contact on August 27, more than 24 hours after a deadly flood tore through the border region with Tibet. Afp Contributor#afp/AFP via Getty Images

U.S. President Donald Trump was asked about the Americans currently impacted by the deadly Nepal floods in the Oval Office Thursday. He called the disaster a "terrible thing" and said the U.S. is in active communication with Nepal's leadership and has offered to provide as much aid as necessary.

"That's a terrible thing. No, we are sending aid, and we've spoken to the leadership, and we let them know anything they want will happen," Trump said.

ABC News' Desiree Adib, Somayeh Malekian, Emily Chang, Will Gretzky, Charlotte Gardiner, Shannon Kingston, Ivan Pereira, Daniel Manzo, Joseph Simonetti, Dada Jovanovic, Chris Boccia, Meghan Mistry and Othon Leyva contributed to this report.

title: Georgia mom among Americans missing in Nepal following deadly floods
content:
Sept. 1, 2026, 3:26 p.m. ET

A glacier collapse and mudslide in the Himalayas caused a catastrophic and cascading flood in Nepal, and thousands of people remain missing as the death toll rises.

More than 2,500 people are unaccounted for, and nearly 800 people have died in Nepal as of Aug. 30. An additional 16 people have died and nearly 550 are missing across the border in China, USA TODAY reported.

Dozens of Americans were reported missing by Nepal's tourism board as part of hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area at the time of the flood.

Now, the family of one Canton, Georgia woman is holding out hope that she will be found as rescue officials continue to search through debris left by one of the most severe natural disasters in the region.

Cherokee County family waits for answers

In a rescue flyer shared by 11Alive's Kaitlyn Ross, 60-year-old Mary Sorenson was identified as one of the missing Americans in Nepal.

She was in the country for a Mansarovar pilgrimage, a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar located in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. The trip is typically made by those who practice Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism and Bon, who all hold the location as sacred.

Sorenson was on the trip organized by Isha Sacred Walks and was heading back into Nepal the last time she communicated with her family. Her last known location was at the immigration facility in Gyirong on the Tibet side of the border. She was headed back into Nepal to Kathmandu and eventually Delhi, India to come home. She was last known to be at that location at 9 a.m. local time on Aug. 26.

Videos of the immigration center taken the same morning show devastation as flood waters crashed into building and swept away people and roads.

In an interview with WSB-TV, Sorenson's son said she had texted her family that morning thanking them for the trip and saying she had a great experience.

"She was able to hike up to an incredible mountain with incredible views and swim in an incredible lake and experience all these amazing things that she felt would help her get closer to God and experience God's grace," Riley Wildeman told the outlet. "The group that she was with was able to confirm that she was in the immigration center at the time that everything happened."

According to 11Alive, Sorenson and her husband, Brian, were active in the Canton community, and Brian was known as the retired Captain of the Cherokee County Fire and Emergency Services.

What caused the Nepal flood?

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, what was first thought to be an earthquake was actually the slope failure of a massive glacier in the Himalayan Mountains that created energy equivalent to an M5.2 earthquake. The rumble caused debris and water to flood as far as 62 miles south. A second seismic event was recorded three hours later at a force of an M4.2 earthquake, but officials are still unsure whether the initial slope failure caused the second event as a landslide, or if it was also caused by glacial collapse.

"A glacial collapse is where a portion of a glacier breaks off, and the debris rapidly moves downslope. The glacial debris contained water and ice that rapidly melted, picking up more material and water as it flowed downslope in the existing stream and river channels, creating a fast-moving, far-traveled landslide and flood laden with boulders and other rubble," according to USGS.

Irene Wright is the Atlanta Connect reporter with USA Today’s Deep South Connect team. Find her on X @IreneEWright or email her at ismith@usatodayco.com.

title: Why This Weekend’s Nor’easter Is Like a Hurricane
author: Dennis Mersereau
content:
A powerful nor’easter developing this week will bring wicked winds, rough surf, and heavy rains to coastal communities from North Carolina to Nova Scotia.

These types of storms are more synonymous with mid-winter than mid-fall. And true to form, this storm is a little different. It won’t drop snow or ice like a classic winter nor’easter. In fact, this system may bring a tease of tropical weather to an Atlantic basin that’s been devoid of hurricane activity so far this year.

An Impactful Nor’easter for the East Coast

Nor’easters are special types of low-pressure systems that earn their name from the fierce northeasterly winds that can lash coastlines.

The seed that’ll grow into this weekend’s nor’easter started developing on Wednesday a few hundred miles off North Carolina’s Outer Banks. The system will meander toward New England into this weekend before slowly winding down into early next week.

Forecasters expect strong, persistent winds to hit coastal locations from North Carolina to Nova Scotia. The strongest gusts will buffet New England through Friday and Saturday, when winds may reach 60 to 70 mph.

Communities throughout the region can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion, life-threatening rip currents, and dangerously rough surf. Isolated power outages are possible. Flight delays at New York's and Boston’s airports are also likely due to blustery winds and rain.

Computer models still don’t entirely agree on how close to the coast this storm will track, or how long it’ll linger in the area—both factors that are crucial to determining exact impacts. A slower track closer to the coast will plaster the region with stronger winds and heavier rainfall than a faster path or one that keeps the center of the storm farther out to sea.

Nor’easters Are Common in Late Fall and Winter

Nor’easters are most common between October and April as powerful jet streams sweep across North America. It’s unusual for such a potent nor’easter to develop this early in the season.

Nor’easters are considered non-tropical—or as meteorologists call them, extratropical—systems that typically draw most of their energy from intense upper-level winds. That’s different from hurricanes, which tend to feed on warmer-than-normal oceans. But low-pressure systems exist on a spectrum that sometimes makes it difficult to neatly define them as tropical or extratropical, and this storm is a prime example.

A Tropical Connection

Some computer models suggest that this week’s nor’easter may acquire some tropical characteristics as it intensifies off the Northeast coastline. Fully extratropical systems feature cold air throughout the entire core of the storm. This nor’easter, on the other hand, may briefly develop a shallow warm core, a phenomenon found in tropical storms and hurricanes. Cloud structure, the storm’s overall wind field, and thunderstorm activity near its center are other tropical characteristics to watch out for.

Even though it’s not likely to earn a name as a hurricane would, it’s important for residents throughout the region to pay attention to the threat of flooding, wind damage, and power outages.

It’s strangely fitting that a nor’easter may prove to be the most hurricane-like non-hurricane we’ve seen across the Atlantic basin this season. We’re now past the peak of hurricane season and the year remains historically quiet. Tropical activity here is running at less than 10 percent of normal for this point in the year. This is also the latest the season has gone without producing a hurricane since the satellite era began in 1966. A quiet hurricane season is a hallmark of an El Niño, when hot waters in the tropical Pacific create conditions in the atmosphere unsuitable for tropical storms to form in the Atlantic.

But winter is a different story, and this week’s storm is also a potential preview of what’s to come as El Niño gains strength. Strong El Niño events tend to influence an active storm track across the southern US during the cooler months, which may in turn lead to more coastal storms along the Eastern Seaboard.

title: 'No doubt' that climate change led to Nepal-Tibet flood, study finds
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Nepal plans to use a new study linking climate change to the deadly floods last month as the basis of a financial request from a United Nations fund.

The BBC understands that Nepal hopes to claim around $20m (£15m) from the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which helps countries affected by climate change.

Around 1,400 people have died in the disaster while 6,150 people remain missing in Nepal as of Wednesday, according official data.

The study by research group World Weather Attribution, published on Thursday, says climate change was a likely contributing factor in the avalanche of rock and ice that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border last month.

There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Dr Friederike Otto, an Imperial College London climatologist who co-authored the study.

Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing.

Scientists say the floods were caused by a collapse of rock wall and glacier ice near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.

The study said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses

According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (2.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate".

Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability.

Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year.

Climate change, while not the only cause of the disaster, was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", the study said.

In the wake of the floods, Nepal's leaders have said the country needs around $5bn (£3.7bn) to rebuild itself.

The UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which came into operation last year, requires countries to submit evidence proving that the losses they faced were caused by climate change.

Nepali officials had been preparing satellite and drone images, as well as preliminary reports, to back up its request to the fund.

But the World Weather Attribution report is now the strongest evidence for their claim that climate change was a significant factor in the collapse of rock and ice at Langtang Lirung, authorities say.

The report "will be the main basis of our claim as it has detailed what role climate has played in this disaster," said Maheshwar Dhakal, spokesperson for Nepal's Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.

title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.

Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.

"It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.

The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.

"I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.

title: Floods hit a historic Grand Canyon lodge. It’s the second park landmark affected by a natural disaster in the past year
author: Chris Boyette
content:
The Grand Canyon’s vast, mile-deep landscape may appear timeless, but two devastating disasters have recently struck the iconic natural wonder as the climate crisis intensifies extreme weather.

Muddy brown floodwaters roared through Phantom Ranch on August 29, swamping the 1920s lodge that has welcomed adventurers seeking a rare chance to spend the night at the bottom of the Grand Canyon and making it the park’s second historic structure impacted by a natural disaster in just over a year.

In July 2025, a destructive wildfire tore through dense pines on the canyon’s northern edge, destroying the historic Grand Canyon Lodge — the park’s only lodging there. The disastrous late-August flash flooding near Phantom Ranch struck below the burn scar left by that blaze, the National Weather Service said.

The climate crisis is making certain types of extreme weather events both more frequent and more severe. A warmer atmosphere can hold more water, which it wrings out in the form of more intense rainfall in some regions, potentially leading to devastating flooding. It’s also loading the dice in favor of wildfires that burn longer and hotter. In turn, landscapes marred by fire are more susceptible to flash flooding, due to sparse vegetation and changes in the soil.

Ahead of the normally busy Labor Day weekend at the park, the scars of these natural disasters and subsequent closures of lodging and hiking trails will likely impact how visitors enjoy one of America’s most iconic landscapes during the holiday and for years to come.

Floodwaters swamp a remote refuge at the bottom of the Grand Canyon

Cabins at Phantom Ranch are seen in 2006. Michael Quinn/National Park Service

Tucked beside the Bright Angel Creek, nearly a mile below the canyon rim, Phantom Ranch was built in 1922. Construction was carried out mostly by foot and mules, as documented by historical photographs from the National Park Service.

To this day, there are no roads leading to the ranch. Guests arrive only by a 7.5-to-10-mile hike, mule ride or rafting down the Colorado River, making it one of the most remote and sought-after reservations in the National Park system, with reservations available via an online lottery 15 months in advance.

The stone cabins and canteen made of rounded river rocks showcase the rustic, homey appeal of the campground, whose outward appearance had changed little since 1922, according to the NPS.

People enjoy a swimming pool at Phantom Ranch in 1961. Merrill D. Beal/National Park Service

The remote ranch’s hallmark isolation is now complicating recovery efforts.

As the murky waters of Bright Angel Creek began to retreat after the floods, witnesses described debris-filled water carrying mud, rocks and fallen trees through the canyon, transforming the area surrounding the ranch.

Floods destroyed the footbridges, leaving remnants of stone pylons littering the creek, NPS said, and hiking trails, utilities and other infrastructure suffered significant damage.

Remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek are seen in this image released by the National Park Service on Sunday. J. Thompson/National Park Service/AFP via Getty Images

The aftermath of the flash flood is seen at Bright Angel Creek near the Phantom Ranger Station on Saturday. Parth Desai via AP

The ranch, the nearby Bright Angel Campground and large sections of the inner canyon trail network remain closed indefinitely.

The NPS is cleaning up the campground and assessing damage to facilities and infrastructure across the area, but it is too soon to determine the extent of the damage at Phantom Ranch, the Interior Department said in a statement to CNN.

Two people were killed in the flooding, and another hiker remains missing.

After the flood, 62 people were evacuated from the campground and the lower North Kaibab Trail, according to the NPS.

Campers enjoy the Bright Angel Campground in the Grand Canyon in this image taken in 2010. Michael Quinn/National Park Service

One factor that may have limited the disaster’s toll was the closure of the ranch’s hiker dormitories. The bunkhouses had been closed since early 2020 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent infrastructure projects, with one men’s dorm and one women’s dorm scheduled to reopen September 1. Had they been full, more hikers could have been caught in the rising waters.

A wildfire destroyed the park’s sole North Rim lodging

The Dragon Bravo Fire burns on the north side of Grand Canyon National Park on July 11, 2025. Grand Canyon National Park via Getty Images

A lightning strike on July 4, 2025, sparked a blaze fueled by hot temperatures, low humidity and strong winds that raced across the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park. Within days, it had destroyed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

Park officials initially expressed little concern about the fire at the less-visited North Rim, which draws only about a tenth of the Grand Canyon’s millions of annual visitors. But by July 13, the Dragon Bravo Fire had grown out of control, destroying 85% of the lodge and its outbuildings, according to the NPS.

Grand Canyon Lodge employees gather for a "sing-away" ceremony for leaving visitors in 1949. Eden/National Park Service

Visitors enjoy the view from the Grand Canyon Lodge in 2007. Michael Quinn/National Park Service

When the lodge burned down in 2025, it wasn’t the first time. First built in 1928, the lodge burned down in a kitchen fire in 1932 and was rebuilt in 1937, according to the Grand Canyon Historical Society. The new building used much of the original lodge’s native Kaibab Limestone, according to the NPS.

Located at the end of Arizona’s Highway 67, the Grand Canyon Lodge welcomed travelers and was often their first sight in the park — even before the canyon itself, the NPS said.

Its sloped roof and large ponderosa beams made it a landmark on the North Rim.

The NPS said long-term recovery planning is underway, but no reopening date has been announced for the historic lodge.

One famous resident of the lodge survived the flames. Brighty the Burro, a 600-pound bronze statue that greeted visitors in the Grand Canyon Lodge, was found damaged by the fire, but park officials chose to save the cherished mascot.

The statue was modeled after a real burro that lived in the canyon in the early 20th century. According to the Grand Canyon Historical Society, the animal gave children rides and hauled water to a North Ridge summer camp in exchange for pancakes.

Brighty is being kept safe at the Grand Canyon Museum Collection facility, the NPS said, with no timeline yet for his restoration or return to the North Rim.

title: Apple Pledges Donation for Nepal and Tibet Flood Relief
author: Hartley Charlton
content:
Apple CEO Tim Cook today pledged that the company will make a donation toward relief and rebuilding work in Nepal and Tibet, where flash floods and mudslides have killed hundreds of people.



On Wednesday, part of a Himalayan glacier collapsed, briefly damming a river before a surge of water and mud hit communities downstream. Many people are dead or missing, and roads, bridges, and homes near the Nepal–Tibet border have been destroyed.

Our thoughts are with all those affected by the tragic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal and Tibet. Apple is making a donation to support relief and rebuilding efforts on the ground. — Tim Cook (@tim_cook) August 28, 2026

This marks Apple's fifth disaster relief pledge in just over two months, after the company supported Indonesia's earthquake recovery earlier this month and previously stepped in for crises in Venezuela, Southern Europe, and Japan.

Cook makes this pledge in the final days of his tenure as CEO. John Ternus takes over the role on September 1, when Cook will shift into the newly created executive chairman position, where he is expected to continue representing Apple on policy matters.

title: Nepal-Tibet flood death toll rises to 750, officials say, more than 3,000 missing
author: Abc News
content:
Approximately 85 Americans were still among the missing as of Sunday.

Nepal-Tibet flood death toll rises to 797, officials say, more than 3,000 missing

LONDON -- The death toll from last week's flash flooding disaster in the Nepal-Tibet border region rose to nearly 800 people as of Sunday, according to the latest updates from Nepali and Chinese officials.

At least 781 bodies had been recovered in Nepal as of Sunday, the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority said in a post to X. At least 2,502 people are still missing, the authority said.

On the other side of the border, China's state-run Xinhua News Agency said that at least 16 people had been confirmed killed. Another 546 people were still missing, Xinhua reported.

At least 85 Americans were still among the missing as of Sunday, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told ABC News' Martha Raddatz Sunday on "This Week." Nine Americans total had been evacuated, Pigott said, up from five on Friday.

Rescue works continue at Trishuli Center in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Aug. 30, 2026. Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty Images

"Our priority is the safety and security of the American people. As you mentioned, the remoteness of this location makes getting reliable information difficult. But our dedication remains," Pigott added. "We have activated from the State Department $3.6 million in emergency humanitarian assistance that includes up to three months of emergency food for up to 10,000 flood-affected households."

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district along the border with Tibet at around 8:40 a.m. local time Wednesday, authorities said. The flooding inundated areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

The deadly wall of water that descended from the mountains on the border between Nepal and Tibet caused destruction at least 62 miles downriver from the border in Nepal, an ABC News analysis of verified video and satellite images shows.

This graphic shows destruction along the path of a landslide and subsequent flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border. Felt Maps/ABC News

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 12 miles northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China frontier, according to Nepal Disaster Management.

A 5.2-magnitude landslide was registered in Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The initial location of the glacier was a cliff about 16,000 feet high. The debris avalanche, or landslide, slid down 6,000 feet on the slope, the USGS said.

ABC News' Rashid Haddou contributed to this report.
